title: Apply health and safety principles in horticulture

lessons.title: Hazards in horticulture and protective clothing
lessons.html:
Hazards in horticulture and protective clothing

Working in gardens and nurseries looks easy, but there are many dangers. A hazard is anything that can hurt you. The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 says the employer must make work safe, and you must work safely, follow the rules and report dangers.

Common hazards

HazardExample
MachinesMowers, brushcutters, hedge trimmers, chainsaws
Sharp toolsSecateurs, saws, spades, knives
ChemicalsPesticides, herbicides, fertiliser
LiftingHeavy pots, bags of compost, paving
Sun and heatSunburn, heatstroke, dehydration
Animals and insectsBees, wasps, snakes, spiders, dogs
ElectricityCables, pumps, buried wires
Slips and tripsWet paving, hoses, holes

Personal protective equipment (PPE)

  • Safety boots: protect toes from tools, machines and heavy pots.
  • Gloves: protect hands from thorns, cuts, soil and chemicals.
  • Safety glasses: protect eyes from stones and chips.
  • Ear plugs or muffs: protect ears from loud machines.
  • Hat, long sleeves and sunscreen: protect from the sun.
  • Overall: protects skin and clothes.
  • Dust mask or respirator: when the job or chemical label says so.

Look after your PPE. Tell your team leader if it is broken. Broken PPE does not protect you.

Look before you start

Before every job, stop and look around for one minute. Ask yourself: What can hurt me here? Is there a wasp nest in the hedge? Is the ground wet and slippery? Are there children or pets nearby? Is there a cable near where I will dig? If you see a danger you cannot fix, tell your team leader before you start work.

lessons.title: Safe work, chemicals and first aid
lessons.html:
Safe work, chemicals and first aid

Safe ways of working

  • Use tools only for their job. Carry sharp tools pointing down.
  • Never remove guards from machines.
  • Only use machines you have been trained on.
  • Lift with bent knees and a straight back. Get help for heavy things.
  • Drink water often on hot days. Rest in the shade.
  • Keep paths clear of hoses and tools.
  • Look before you put your hand into a bush or under a pot. Snakes and spiders hide there.

Chemicals

  • Only trained workers may mix or spray chemicals.
  • Read the label. It says which PPE to wear.
  • Never eat, drink or smoke when working with chemicals.
  • Never put chemicals in cool drink bottles.
  • Keep chemicals locked in the store.
  • Wash hands and face after work.

Reporting

Tell your team leader at once about any injury, even a small cut. Also report dangers like a broken ladder, a wasp nest or a loose cable. Reporting can stop someone else from getting hurt.

Basic first aid

Know where the first aid box is and who the first aider is.

  • Small cut: wash with clean water, cover with a plaster. Wear gloves when helping others.
  • Bleeding: press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth and call the first aider.
  • Chemical on skin or in eyes: rinse with lots of clean water for a long time. Take the label to the clinic.
  • Bee sting: scrape the sting out. If the person has trouble breathing or swelling of the face, call for emergency help at once.
  • Snake bite: keep the person calm and still, do not cut or suck the bite, and get them to hospital fast.
  • Heatstroke: move to shade, cool with water, call for help.

This is only basic information. Hands-on first aid training by an accredited provider is required before you act as a first aider.

Key points

  • A hazard is anything that can hurt you; know the hazards at work.
  • Wear the right PPE and report broken PPE.
  • Only trained workers use machines and chemicals.
  • Report every injury and danger at once.
  • Know the first aid box and the first aider; get proper first aid training.
